It has been a very, very long time since I have been so profoundly moved by a film like I was with this one. Sadly the best way I can describe such an intense melding of story, acting, visuals, pacing and sound is with the very tired cliche of "masterpiece". Moonlight, the Oscar winning best picture in 2017, is an unapologetic masterpiece. Watching it is like staring at a canvas by Picasso or Pollock and imagining you get to see if from the first drop of paint through its finality. It's often messy, continually fluid, and always mesmerizing.

The movie follows a character named Chiron in three distinct phases of his life… childhood, teen years and adulthood. His attempts to find connection with other people are most often hindered by circumstances and conditions beyond his own control. Alex Hibbert, Ashton Sanders and Trevante Rhodes are each phenomenal in bringing Chiron to life through these three phases. Naomie Harris as Chiron's mother and Mahershala Ali as Juan both turn in performances worthy of the Oscar nominations they both received (Ali took home the award for Best Supporting Actor).

Directed by Barry Jenkins, appropriately an Oscar nominee as well, this film is one best left to unfold itself individually to each viewer. To present the specifics and nuances of the story or storytelling would be a disservice to anyone that is interested in watching a superlative film. Best you watch and see how it makes you feel, free of any preconceived conclusions.

This movie will both uplift, and haunt me, for a long time.

Moonlight is a coming of age story about a young black man named Chiron.  The story leads the viewer through 3 stages of his life, growing up in a rough and dangerous neighbourhood in Miami.  Living with his drug addict mother he finds solace with a local drug dealer who becomes a father figure to him and offers a hideaway for him against the life his mother inflicts on him and the bullies who terrorise him at school because of his sexuality. Growing up he struggles to accept the person he is, choosing to live alone rather than give in to what he truly feels.
Moonlight was an excellent portrayal of a young man struggling with who he is and who society expects him to be.  It was a restrained and subtle performance from the 3 young actors who lead the film which worked well with the tone of the movie as a whole.  Naomi Harris was exceptionally good playing Chiron's mother, she was completely unrecognisable from any other role she has played.  I also felt the film worked well avoiding any expected cliches , especially with the character Juan, played brilliantly by Mahershala Ali.  It would have been very easy to have him play a stereotype but he was a well written character with hidden and unexpected depths.  Worth watching for a slightly different take on the coming of age story.

Back in 2017, I remember the Oscar fiasco, as I'm sure everyone does. At the time, I was incredibly supportive of Lala Land, and mad that Moonlight took the best picture spot. But, now that I've actually watched both movies, I think it's clear Moonlight deserved it. Interestingly, Moonlight is adapted from a stage play of the same name. The structures of film and stage are completely different, so, it's miraculous that the writing was as good as it was in this film. While there are certain sections of the film that could have been adapted further, for the most part, things were adapted well. One thing that stays the same, are the characters. Each character in Moonlight is distinct and, even though many are played by multiple actors, have a distinct and unique voice and feel. This is supported by some excellent acting, the standout performance obviously being Mahershala Ali. Although his role is brief, him being a sort of father figure to Little is spectacular. The film deals with some heavy material. And, while I definitely feel that it should have taken some time to breath, I also understand why the life of Little seems as tortuous as it appears. The film's distinction also comes in its visual style, at the beginning, the way it was shot feels like a distant memory. But, as Little grows up, getting less little (I couldn't help myself), the way everything is shot seems much less fuzzy. As things in Little's world start to make sense for him, the make sense for us. This just adds to how important the characters in this are, which is interesting, there are maybe only three or four characters with speaking roles, likely something transferred over from the play. Overall, I definitely liked this movie quite a bit, but, I also found that due to it being adapted from a stage play, there were some things that were missing.

Don't take this the wrong way, but I'm generally not a big fan of LGBTQ films because, speaking as a dumb straight dude, I don't understand them. So, as you can see, I wasn't looking forward to seeing Moonlight, a film focused on an African American boy from Miami who ventures through age as he experiences homosexuality, physical and emotional abuse. The first part where it explores Chiron's childhood was probably the best part of the movie. I really rooted for the kid as he clings to Juan (Mahershala Ali) to hide from his mother (Naomie Harris), who spouts out abuse on him and hollers the f-word at him. I also loved the connection between him and his best friend Kevin, up to a point where the relationship was more platonic than romantic. However, I know Moonlight the movie and play was supposedly based on the playwright's childhood, but the homoerotic and homophobic scenes came out as cringy and forced. The one scene where Chiron kisses Kevin and gets a felatio felt more like it was done out of pity than a start of the former's homosexual journey. Speaking of, I was surprised to see the homosexuality toned down in the movie, focusing more on Chiron's friendship and reconciliation with family than his sexual turmoil. I guess the studio wanted the film to be more commercially accessible by limiting those themes, but I expected a climactic sex scene that tied all loose ends. Despite my low expectations, Moonlight worked as a coming-of-age family drama, but failed as a LGBTQ film.

Moonlight takes the spot for my second favorite movie of all time. The concept/theme is interesting but the way it's executed is out of this world and makes that concept/theme so much deeper and more engaging. The writing, directing and acting are all great and this is a movie that proves that you don't need to have a total A-list cast to make a fantastic and Academy award winning movie; the only actor in this movie who I knew before seeing it was Mahershala Ali, who gave a phenomenal performance and deserved the Academy award that he won for his work in the movie. Chiron is a unique and complex character and it's really engaging to watch how his personality affects him and his relationships with those he cares about as he grows up. The structure of this movie is also really cool, as it's divided into 3 sections that each detail a part of Chiron's life and how he changes as he goes from a boy to a teenager to an adult while still remaining the same in many ways. This is a film that showcases that no matter how old you get or how much mental development you go through, you'll still be the same person in a lot of ways. The way that the movie flows and transitions through these 3 sections is great and doesn't feel disruptive to it at all or cause any awkward or abrupt moments. Another thing that makes this movie more unique and complex than it may appear at first glance is how the movie is described in a google search. You'll see it as "Gay & lesbian/Drama" or "Drama/LGBT" and a synopsis will talk about falling in love. I definitely agree with the drama, and it's undeniable that Chiron is a gay character, but this movie isn't about romance or LGBTQ related themes. It certainly includes them and makes sure we know about them, but Moonlight is really a coming of age story that's rare and underrepresented in cinema and that's part of what makes this movie as good as it is. I'm sure that there are people in the real world who have stories similar to that of Chiron and yet we never hear about any of them. Moonlight is a film about stories we don't normally hear or care about. The struggle that Chiron goes through is a product of his upbringing and the environment that surrounds him throughout his life, and it's a struggle that I'm sure so many other people will be able to relate to. In part two of the film there were many depressing moments during his teenage years, his mom verbally abuses him numerous times throughout this part of the movie, Whenever these incidents occur, the camera goes into the point of view of Chiron and everything zones out, with his mom distortedly tantruming and screaming in front of him. Giving you that point of view helps you take in every facial expression and understand how sedimental this visit really is. Wanted to see as many 2016 films as possible, especially those that won or were nominated for the big awards. Took me a while to see 'Moonlight', with the controversy it garnered when it was announced for the Best Picture Oscar and the amount of hate it's got here part of me was wary.

Finally getting round to seeing 'Moonlight', it turned out that it was more than well worth the while and that the wariness was not needed. 'Moonlight' is not a perfect film and may not have been my personal pick for the Best Picture award (for me that was 'La La Land' though that is not a popular opinion it seems). Truly admired what it set out to do and found it a brave and powerful film, despite what the detractors say there is far more to 'Moonlight's' appeal than politics, sexuality and race (clearly trying to find conspiracy theories and reasons for why a film they dislike is loved by others, without taking into account that the film simply just connected to and resonated with those who liked it).

'Moonlight' does end on an anti-climactic note, some of the last act is a bit rushed. A longer length would have helped as a result, it also would have helped make a couple of events in the first act a little clearer and not so choppy.

It may not say much new, despite the ground-breaking concept on paper with the exploration of lives rarely seen on film, and doesn't always have subtlety. Then again it is tackling far from subtle themes and a heavy subject, so that sort of was going to be inevitable.

However, 'Moonlight' is an exceptionally well made film. The cinematography and editing are some of the most eye-pleasing and best of that year, and can't find anything to fault the expertly handled direction. The music is cleverly mixed and has haunting power and fluidity.

Regarding the writing, it is not perfect, at times as said a little heavy-handed and vague in parts, but it is thought-provoking and handles very ambitious, relevant, important themes with power, truth and (mostly) delicacy. The story makes the most of the three act structure, it's handled simply but not simplistically and also handled cleverly and with passion, honesty and intelligence. Found myself relating quite a lot to and being moved significantly by the story and found the film handled a heavy and sensitive subject matter with a lot of relevance and importance today more than admirably.

Can't fault the acting, doing wonders with compellingly real characters and strongly defined character relationships (especially the central one). Much has been made of Maharshala Ali and Naomie Harris and deservedly with two of the best performances that year, Ali especially is extraordinary. It is easy though to overlook Alex R. Hibbert, Trevante Rhodes and Ashton Sanders and one shouldn't, as they are just as worthy (particularly Sanders).

Juan was a drug dealer who hadn't read much, but what he meant was that everyone has their own nature, which is what you are in the moonlight, and that a person must live their own nature rather than follow the crowd. However, in the actual world, how much we have experienced and how many people we have encountered has changed our color, to the point where we still live in the color that others have given us, and we have even forgotten our original color.

Chiron lives in a bad single-parent family. His mother was a drug addict and promiscuous, and instead of bringing motherly love to the child, she often scolded and made the little Chiron do a lot of menial work, and from the very beginning, he had no good impression of women. On the contrary, the two men he met as a teenager brought him a lot of positive influence, which may be an important factor in changing his sexual orientation. Like a father, Juan gives Chiron love and care, and more importantly, he guides Chiron to develop his own independent personality. An important part of the film is when Juan teaches Chiron how to swim, saying "you should relax and trust yourself" while telling him "I will hold you up". Until one day, Chiron asked Juan, "Are you a drug dealer?" The first day, Juan nodded honestly, Chiron disregarded Juan's long-time love and care, very ungrateful slammed the door, and left. In fact, this is the formation of Chiron's independent personality, he is not bound by the values of this society to know the return, but to show their own nature, of course, this young impulse, the spontaneity, but also for him to pay the price later laid the groundwork.

Kevin is a real friend of Chiron. It is not difficult to imagine, living in such a family of boys, how inferior, coupled with physical weakness, poor communication, Chiron is often bullied by the children. This is when Kevin stood up for Chiron and told him that he should fight back and stop letting people think he was a bully because Kevin knew deep down that Chiron was a strong person. So, the two children wrestled together, in this wrestling full of care and understanding, Chiron's heartfelt the good things, perhaps at this point, he to the male, to Kevin sprouted a good feeling, although not necessarily considered love.

The circumstances of young Chiron's life did not change much, still being bullied and not getting a bit of love from his mother. Although Juan has died, Chiron has learned from Juan's tough nature, he is still often to Juan's girlfriend Teresa's home to feel the only good in his life. Although Teresa was a beautiful and kind woman, because of Juan's high status in Chiron's heart, he treated Teresa with the respect of a mother. Her image of women has always been as distant as that of her biological mother and Teresa, and because of being bullied by the school bullies, from their vulgar insults filled him with disgust for women, and the only time he witnessed sex, it was not even a good impression. Instead, his knowledge of sexual goodness is all learned from Kevin, from Juan's hugs. Finally, at a time when his life is desperate, Kevin comforts him and once again shows him the beauty of life.

This is followed by the climactic part of the film. The school bully encourages Kevin to beat up Chiron, and the young Kevin is forced by social pressure to look at his heart and beat Chiron against his will. But Chiron retains his inner nature and stands strong. So the director used a special set of camera language to show us a coward who is afraid to face his own, a punch on a strong teenager, again and again, knocked down, and again and again, he stood up. Each of these punches is hitting Kevin, who is strong on the outside and weak on the inside, and each one shatters the goodness inside Chiron, and each one makes Chiron more determined to be who he is. When the teacher wanted to help him call the police, he was confident that he was clearly aware of the existence of self-independence from society, he just repeated "you do not know, you do not understand", a person's strength is not shown on the outside like the teacher said swinging fists to retaliate, but the inner resistance to social pressure. He did not hate Kevin, he just broke his heart, so he took out his hatred for society and life on the school bullies who repeatedly bullied him. This is the youth that dares to love and hate. However, impulsiveness comes at a cost

The middle-aged Chiron appearance changed a person. Big steel teeth, gold necklaces, dark strong muscles, subwoofer sports car, he became another Juan. Yet deep inside he is still the same Chiron who was terrified by his mother as a child, still awakened again and again by such nightmares, his skin still blue in the moonlight. A conversation with his mother once again awakened the heart of this fierce drug dealer, and when he accepted his mother's apology, he did not say perfunctorily, "I love you, Mom!" Instead, he truly said what he had been hiding inside for years, "I hate you, Mom!" Then, he hugged his mother in tears, this time he and his mother really love each other, just not hanging on the lips.

The rest of the story, needless to say, is that a Kevin who looks at his own heart has the courage to call Chiron, he apologizes, he regrets, and he saves Chiron when he is lost in the social life, and Chiron gradually sheds his steel teeth, gets rid of the black society has given him, and evokes the blue inside, he overcomes life and retains his innocence.

The quality supporting roles are just as important, with Mahershala Ali in his Academy Award winning role, Naomi Harris as the character's drug-addicted mother, Janelle Monáe as an adult friend, and the three actors playing Kevin, a friend since childhood, in the three stages. Race, sexuality, poverty, and city life are, but it's how they're displayed that makes it a true original.

Covering three stages of a young man's life – childhood, the teenage years, adulthood – Moonlight is the story of Chiron, raised in Miami by a drug-addicted mother in a world of violence and hate. Let me get this out the way first, Moonlight is a well written, well-acted, and well told story about identity in my opinion of course. Now that that's out of the way, I couldn't help but feel I've seen this before. I'll unpack that last statement soon, but first I'll discuss the production quality.

The cinematography was very good. The camera was very loose and fluid in a bunch allowing for sweeps, pans, and overall movement that allowed the movie to feel grounded, funny enough. Certain compositions stood out to me, mostly the close-ups of characters where they are centered.

The lighting for many interior shots gave certain scenes a dream-like quality to them.

The soundtrack was subtle, but the parts of it I loved the absolute most were the multiple renditions of 'Little's Theme' throughout. This beautifully gentle and peaceful piano piece, that starts off tender and shy, then becomes 'Chiron's Theme' and becomes deeper in tone with the same melody, and finally it becomes this confused violin piece in 'Black's Theme'. Each rendition just spoke to what Little was going through in the film, at first he was small and innocent, then growing up, and finally he was confused about who he really is.

Licensed music parts were good too, with the first song lyrics we hear in the film being 'Every ni**a is a star' I felt spoke to partly what this film was trying to say. And the use of Classic Man spoke to what Black was trying to feel for himself.

The characters were well written and acted. I genuinely have nothing more to add to that statement. No one really stood out to me, as everyone worked well together I felt.

The story was fine too. Once again, that's my genuine take there, nothing more to add.

A story about this young boy who is bullied at school (for being gay) with a rough childhood and parents who aren't really there for him, he finds some older person who looks after them and acts a second parent, the boy has a childhood friend who is the only constant good thing for them throughout and who really understands (them) and vice versa, at some point the bullying gets out of hand, and the kid is sent to the principle's office and is reluctant to give up the names of the aggressors out of fear of them, the boy shares some "romantic" and tender moment (maybe while smoking and outside) with the childhood friend (and maybe looses their virginity). Even the ending where they meet up again int the future and things seem like they haven't changed between them.

The storyline regarding Little/Chiron/Blacks sexuality was also very bare bones to be honest. He's gay and shy, gets bullied, but this one guy who seems like a real Chad is the only one who he's really cool with in some way and then they stare into each other's eyes, kiss, then the Chad boy tries to hide his true feelings by doing something with the bullies that he doesn't want to, but does because he has a reputation to uphold.

I just feel like I've seen this before, I don't know. Barry Jenkins directs this Academy award-winning film that follows the emotional story of a young man's struggle to discover himself. The film covers 15 years of Chiron's life as he matures from child to adult. Viewers only see the key/defining points of Chiron's upbringing over the 111 minutes.
 
All three actors that portray Chiron (Alex R Hibbert Ashton Sanders, Trevante Rhodes) each give sensational performances. Despite never meeting one another, they all share a sense of timidness when playing Chiron. Considering 'Moonlight' was Alex R Hibbert's film debut, his talent is tremendous, and his performance radiates a sense of maturity, despite his age. Even though he only appears in the first chapter of the film, Mahershala Ali gives an incredible performance as Juan. Ali's supporting actor Oscar makes him the first person of Muslim faith to win an Academy Award. As well as sharing personality traits, the casting department does a great job making sure each actor that played Chiron looked the same, which is evident in the actors that play Kevin (Jaden Piner, Jharrel Jerome, André Holland).
 
'Moonlight' is an incredible film because it deals with complex themes that are not explored as much as they should be. Themes like identity, black masculinity and sexuality are dominant throughout the film as it progresses. The film also demonstrates how certain moments in your life define you and how bonds between people around you can change over time. During the more transformative moments of his life, Chiron is seen interacting with water - whether it be splashing himself with it or swimming in the ocean. It shows how he uses the water to provide him with a sense of comfort and safety during these intense moments. 'Moonlight' explores themes of homosexuality as Chiron begins to discover himself in his formative years as a teenager.
 
There are numerous scenes throughout the film that can't help but stick with the viewer long after they've watched it. For example, the scene with Juan and Chiron in the ocean at the beginning is not only a visual masterpiece, but a scene that also introduces one of the dominant themes in the film. It's done in such a spectacular way that it stays with the viewer. DOP James Laxton provides 'Moonlight' with gorgeous cinematography that, in some scenes, radiates tranquillity and calmness. Mixing the orchestral pieces of music with crisp rap songs shows the delicacy of the film's themes with the location and surroundings of the main character. As well as making history in the acting categories at the Oscars, 'Moonlight' is the first film with an LGBTQ+ protagonist. The film's best picture win also marks A24's first film to win the prestigious award.

If you want to celebrate Pride month by watching more films that explore LGBTQ+ themes, then you should watch films like 'Blue Is the Warmest Colour', 'Portrait of a Lady on Fire' and 'Tangerine'. But if you want to delve into Barry Jenkins' filmography, then films and shows like 'If Beale Street Could Talk' and 'The Underground Railroad' should be on your watchlist.
 
'Moonlight' is a tender film that tugs on viewers heartstrings as they are taken on the defining journey of one man's life. With exquisite storytelling and gorgeous visuals, 'Moonlight' is perfect if you want a film that deals with deep, heavy themes.

The story of Chiron told through three pivotal moments of his life are shown in such rawness and tenderness in Moonlight. Act 1 is a beautiful portrayal of a father-figure delivered by the stunning acting of Mahershala Ali. Act 2 portrays in a gripping manner the struggle Chiron has and his identity and culminates in shock and wonder. While Act 3 penetrates, despite the thick exterior put on by Chiron, we still see the boy inside To the ocean waves, to the floating in the water, Moonlight is a beautiful reflection and artistic expression covering identity, masculinity, and human connection.

Moonlight is a phenomenal work of drama that examines the psychological unrest that unfolds over the course of a person's life as they come to terms with their sexuality while still trying to survive in a harsh underprivileged inner-city environment. How generational trauma is passed down and the inner struggle to maintain your humanity and happiness despite how much life can drag you down. The performances are amazing, with special highlights from Mahershala Ali, Naomie Harris, and the 3 generations of actors who played the protagonist Chiron. The soundtrack cuts deep with its beautifully tragic orchestral strings and piano work, most notably during Chiron's "baptism" in the ocean, his romantic date on the beach, and long self-transformative hard look into the mirror at heat the second act of the film. It's an emotionally powerful LGBT+ film that's a raw depiction of persevering bigotry, finding acceptance in oneself, and forging meaningful relationships no matter how many people, even some of your closest acquaintances or yourself, say otherwise.

Gut wrenching, heartbreaking, hopeful, and exhilarating, Moonlight will touch all your emotions. It will move you to tears and leave you with goosebumps. The ones caused by a cool nighttime breeze flowing gently against your skin.

I first watched this movie shortly after it shockingly won the Best Picture Oscar over heavy favorite LA LA LAND. I appreciated it at the time, but it didn't wow me. Thankfully a revisit put the whole thing in perspective, and I was more emotionally moved and impressed by the performances, particularly the three actors portraying Chiron during the three stages of his life represented here. I was staggered by how fluidly Rhodes, Sanders and Hibbert inhabited the character and how beautifully the performances melded from one to the other. Mahershala Ali won the Oscar and Naomi Harris was nominated, but I would have loved to see one or all of these leading actors receive more awards attention. Actually, Harris' performance as Chiron's drug addicted mom is the only role that felt a little familiar and borderline cliche. Considering the emotions involved, this is a remarkably subtle and often quiet movie, and it's paced rather slowly to allow time to let everything sink in. Jenkins' filmmaking is often almost uncomfortably intimate, and I mean that in the best possible way. And the emotions he elicits aren't brought about by swelling orchestral music or over-emotive acting. Practically every moment here feels real, and this is a perfect example of a movie that may need to be seen twice - or more times - in order to fully appreciate it. It wouldn't have been my choice for Best Picture that year - I would put it behind MANCHESTER BY THE SEA and ARRIVAL - but it's certainly worthy of the win.
